The Great Emigration & Mickiewicz

Adam Mickiewicz Museum

On this spot Adam Mickiewicz died on 26 November 1855 – in the crypt of the house museum you will find a marble slab, a cross and a copy of the poet's death mask.

Theme
The Great Emigration & Mickiewicz
District
Beyoğlu
Period
1855 / 1955 / 1984
Visiting
Open to visitors

The story

The poet who gave Poland its national epic, Pan Tadeusz, arrived in Istanbul barely two months before his death – and died here, on the corner of Tatlı Badem Sokağı, 'Sweet Almond Street'.

Adam Mickiewicz left Paris on 11 September 1855, during the Crimean War. Officially on a French government research mission, he really came to help raise Polish troops to fight alongside the Ottomans against Russia. In October he visited the camp near Burgas of the Sultan's Cossacks, commanded by Michał Czajkowski, known as Sadyk Pasha. There he and his secretary Armand Lévy planned a Jewish legion. In November Mickiewicz, Lévy and Henryk Służalski rented a wooden house in Pera. On 26 November the poet died. His companions spoke of cholera, others later suspected poisoning; the cause was never settled.

Next day a death mask was taken. By tradition the embalmed body lay in the cellar – today's crypt – until 30 December, when it left by ship for France. That day, despite rain and cold, hundreds of people followed the coffin: Poles, other Slavs, Greeks and Levantines. He was buried at Montmorency, and in 1890 moved to Wawel Cathedral in Kraków. In 1861 his eldest son Władysław came looking for the house; a Warsaw magazine reported that the Muslim family then living there let him walk through every room of his father's last home.

The wooden house burned in the great Pera fire of 1870. A few years later the Ratyński family built the present brick house on the plot with a bilingual Polish–French plaque over the door. A museum opened here in 1955. After the lease ran out in 1977, the Turkish government bought the house in 1979 and restored it; on 4 October 1984 a new exhibition by Warsaw's Museum of Literature opened.

How to visit

The museum is about a 10-minute walk from Taksim Square, across Tarlabaşı Boulevard. It is a branch of the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts (Turkish Ministry of Culture and Tourism); the exhibition is the responsibility of the Adam Mickiewicz Museum of Literature in Warsaw, supported by the Polish Consulate General. The official site has listed free admission, and opening hours differ between sources – check both on turkishmuseums.com before you go. Look at the façade first: the memorial plaques above the door include the Ratyński family's. Inside, four floors follow the poet's life, with a room on the Burgas camp; on the ground floor you can take home cards with his poems in many languages. The heart of the house is the crypt below ground: a marble slab marking his 'temporary resting place', a cross, a copy of the death mask and an icon of Our Lady of Ostra Brama. The stairs are steep and narrow and the building is not wheelchair accessible.
